instructions:
INTENT — The email must read like it was written by a person who spent thirty seconds on the prospect's site, not like a template. One idea, one tone, no stock phrases. The prospect is the subject of the sentences: more "you" than "I".

MODEL — Every email follows exactly this form, five one-sentence paragraphs, one blank line between each, then the first name alone. Nothing else:

Hi Christian,

Saw that Razzmic runs performance marketing and HubSpot work for its clients.

If half the emails on a list bounce, the campaign pays for it.

You paste a name and a company, and the verified work email comes back.

1,000 credits free on signup, no card, enough for 100 of them.

Want me to send the link?

Finn

Never write a number list, a section heading, a bullet, or an extra blank line. Never write "Best," "Cheers," "Regards" or any sign-off above the name. The body runs 55 to 75 words. No sentence over 16 words, no word a fourteen-year-old would not know.

THE READER MUST KNOW WHAT IT DOES — A reader who finishes the email and cannot say what the product does has been failed by it. The third sentence exists for exactly that and is never cut, never merged, and never replaced by a benefit. "Credits" mean nothing on their own: the mechanism sentence is what makes the fourth sentence legible.

NO LINK, EVER — No link, no URL, no bare domain, in this email or in any follow-up. The whole sequence exists to earn a reply; the link is sent by hand once they answer. An email containing a link has failed and must be rewritten.

NEVER INTRODUCE YOURSELF — No "I'm Finn from LinkFinder", no "we help teams", no "we work with", no company name anywhere in the body. Say what it does, never who we are. An email that opens a paragraph with who we are has failed and must be rewritten.

SUBJECT — 2 to 4 words, all lowercase, no punctuation. It contains the prospect's company name or their trade, never ours, never "partnership", "collab", "x", "offer", "quick question", and never a first name alone. Examples: "razzmic lead lists", "your list building", "question on razzmic".

FIRST SENTENCE — An observation starting with "Saw that", "On your site," or "You run". It says what the company does, with one precise detail read from the site: a named client type, a specific service, a city. The word "businesses" is banned, as are "bespoke", "tailored", any date, any headcount, any figure, any hiring, and any client the site does not name. Never guess at their working day: "so I imagine list work lands in your day" is banned, and so is every sentence like it. Never a compliment.

SECOND SENTENCE — The problem, in conditional form, never an assertion about how the prospect works. One or the other: "If half the emails on a list bounce, the campaign pays for it." or "If you pay per seat for data you barely use, that adds up."

THIRD SENTENCE — What the product actually does, as a physical action they perform and a thing that comes back, never as a benefit and never as a category. One of: "You paste a name and a company, and the verified work email comes back." or "You give it a LinkedIn URL and the work email and mobile come back." or "You upload a list of names and it comes back with the emails filled in." Never "data enrichment", never "contact data", never "solution", never "platform".

FOURTH SENTENCE — The free account: 1,000 credits, no card. State only what those credits actually buy. A work email costs 10 credits and a mobile number costs 50, so 1,000 credits is 100 work emails, or 20 mobile numbers, or a mix. Never promise a count the grant does not cover, and never imply both can be had in full. Never offer to run the list yourself.

FIFTH SENTENCE — A closed question whose only answer is yes, asking to send the link: "Want me to send the link?" or "Want the link?". No other wording. NEVER write "Open to a chat?", "Open to discussing?", "Worth a quick call?" or anything asking for a slot. No question mark anywhere else in the email.

OFFER — This is a self-serve trial, not a service. Never offer to run a sample, build a list, send results, or do anything on their behalf. Never ask for a call or a slot. Never name a paid price, a plan or a subscription. Never write "AI", never name a competitor, never mention an API, an integration or a dashboard. Never quote a match rate, a coverage percentage or a database size: the hit rate is the objection, so they measure it themselves on their own rows.
followup_instructions:
LENGTH — Two sentences maximum, same shape and same bans as the first email: one sentence per paragraph, a blank line between each, no sentence over 16 words, the first name alone at the end with no sign-off above it.

NO LINK, EVER — Same as the first email. No link, no URL, no bare domain, in any follow-up. The link is sent by hand once they reply. A follow-up containing a link has failed.

BANS — Everything the first email bans, plus the openers. NEVER write "following up", "just following up", "bumping this", "circling back" or "quick nudge". Never introduce yourself, never name the company in the body, never write "AI", never name a competitor, never name a paid price or plan, never quote a match rate or a database size.

WHAT CHANGES — The offer was already made, so a follow-up never repeats it. Add one new fact each time, and keep it concrete in the same way the third sentence was: another input that works, another thing that comes back, a file format, the fact that credits do not expire.

THE ASK — Still the same yes: "Want me to send the link?". Never offer to run a sample, never ask for a call or a slot. The last email asks for a yes or a no, and means it.
